paragraphs: An unusual reading in a collection of time series can involve more than an unexpected value: it can also involve a change in how variables relate to one another. CAROTS builds an anomaly detector around this idea, using causal relationships between variables to shape what its learned representation treats as normal or abnormal.

The method creates two kinds of altered training samples. One preserves causal relationships and supplies varied examples of normal behavior; the other disturbs those relationships to produce synthetic anomalies. Contrastive learning then trains an encoder to distinguish these groups in its internal representation. This makes the distinction between preserved and disrupted relationships part of the training signal.

CAROTS also introduces a similarity-filtered loss that gradually admits more semantically diverse samples sharing causal relationships. This broadens the normal variations considered during learning. Experiments on five real-world and two synthetic datasets support improved anomaly detection from incorporating causal relationships. The findings suggest that how variables interact can provide useful detection information alongside their individual time-series patterns.
icml-2025-causality-aware-contrastive-le.tldr: CAROTS improves time-series anomaly detection by teaching an encoder to distinguish variations that preserve causal relationships from those that disrupt them.

paragraphs: Residual vector quantization represents data through multiple quantization steps, with greater depth supporting higher fidelity. For a generative model, however, that richer representation can require more inference steps. ResGen addresses this tension by changing what the model predicts, allowing deeper quantization without tying the number of generation steps to that depth.

Instead of predicting every token individually, ResGen predicts a vector embedding representing tokens collectively. The central benefit is that its inference-step count remains independent of quantization depth. The paper also gives token masking and simultaneous token prediction a probabilistic formulation using discrete diffusion and variational inference, connecting the generation procedure to a common mathematical framework.

The authors evaluate ResGen on conditional image generation at ImageNet 256-by-256 resolution and zero-shot text-to-speech synthesis. They report better performance than autoregressive counterparts in both settings without sacrificing sampling speed. Increasing quantization depth also yields better generation fidelity or faster sampling than similarly sized baselines. These results support the approach across both image and speech generation, with benefits expressed as quality or speed improvements.
icml-2025-efficient-generative-modeling-.tldr: ResGen predicts collective token embeddings to improve generation quality without making inference-step counts grow with quantization depth.

paragraphs: Fair clustering seeks useful groups while controlling how people or instances from protected groups are distributed among them. Existing approaches can struggle to satisfy fairness requirements without losing clustering quality or encountering numerical instability. This paper proposes Fair Clustering via Alignment, or FCA, based on a new decomposition of the fair K-means objective.

FCA alternates between two operations. It first finds a joint probability distribution that aligns data from different protected groups. It then updates cluster centers in the resulting aligned space. The alignment step handles the relationship between groups, allowing center optimization to proceed without the complex constraints used by other fair clustering approaches.

The theoretical result guarantees approximately optimal clustering utility for a specified fairness level. This concerns the quality attainable at that fairness level, rather than claiming an exact optimum. Experiments report a better fairness–utility trade-off than existing methods and near-perfect fairness without numerical instability. Together, the results present alignment as a practical way to manage fairness requirements while retaining useful cluster structure.
icml-2025-fair-clustering-via-alignment-.tldr: FCA alternates protected-group alignment and cluster-center updates to achieve strong clustering utility at chosen fairness levels.

paragraphs: Understanding a neural population involves explaining how its collective activity evolves, beyond describing individual neurons separately. FINDR uses deep recurrent networks to infer a low-dimensional dynamical description from neural recordings. The inferred dynamics are nonlinear and stochastic, allowing the description to include both structured changes and randomness in population activity.

The authors apply this unsupervised method to spike trains recorded from frontal brain regions of rats performing an auditory decision-making task. FINDR performs competitively with existing methods at capturing the different response patterns of individual neurons. This provides evidence that its compact dynamical representation can retain relevant features of varied neural responses.

When trained to separate activity relevant to the task from irrelevant activity, FINDR reveals interpretable dynamics that can be displayed as flow fields and attractors. These visualizations describe how inferred states evolve and the structures toward which they move. They enable direct tests of attractor-based accounts of neural computation. The paper therefore presents FINDR as a tool for investigating proposed computational mechanisms through interpretable population dynamics.
icml-2025-flow-field-inference-from-neur.tldr: FINDR infers interpretable, low-dimensional neural dynamics that can help test attractor-based theories of brain computation.

paragraphs: Training a language model across geographic regions introduces slow communication links and hardware that completes work at different speeds. HALoS organizes optimization around these differences. It uses local parameter servers within regions and a global parameter server that merges updates across regions, creating a hierarchy for collecting and combining training progress.

This organization takes advantage of faster connections within each region while reducing costly communication between regions. Its asynchronous operation also reduces the effects of slower participants. The paper supplies a convergence analysis for non-convex objectives, including guarantees concerning hierarchical momentum, linking the distributed training design to its optimization behavior.

In the reported experiments, HALoS converges up to 7.5 times faster than synchronous baselines and up to 2.1 times faster than existing asynchronous methods. These are maximum reported improvements, rather than uniform speedups. It also matches or exceeds fully synchronous SGD on language-modeling and downstream benchmark accuracy. The findings show that hierarchical update accumulation and global merging can reduce total training time while preserving model quality in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-halos-hierarchical-asynchronou.tldr: HALoS uses hierarchical asynchronous updates to accelerate geographically distributed language-model training while preserving quality in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Biological sequence design involves searching enormous spaces while limiting expensive evaluations. A proxy model can quickly estimate sequence quality, but limited training data can make its predictions unreliable for unfamiliar candidates. This paper develops a conservative off-policy search procedure intended to keep exploration within regions where those estimates are more trustworthy.

The method begins with high-scoring sequences from offline data. It randomly masks each token with probability delta, then uses the policy to fill in the missing tokens. This creates a controlled way to modify promising existing sequences. The method also adjusts delta for each data point according to proxy uncertainty, matching the degree of conservativeness to the model's confidence.

Experiments cover DNA, RNA, protein, and peptide design. The authors report that the conservative search consistently improves off-policy training and finds higher-scoring sequences than existing machine-learning methods across the evaluated tasks. The contribution is a way to connect exploration directly to uncertainty in the scoring model, addressing a source of unreliability in proxy-guided sequence search.
icml-2025-improved-off-policy-reinforcem.tldr: Delta-Conservative Search improves biological sequence search by adapting masked-token exploration to uncertainty in the proxy scoring model.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection helps identify inputs that differ from the data a model is prepared to handle. Many detectors look for unusual statistical patterns in a neural network's internal representations. This paper adds a probabilistic reasoning component to existing detectors, using relationships between human-understandable concepts as another source of evidence.

The reasoning component is a Markov logic network, which combines logical statements with probabilities. Weighted logical constraints influence the probability assigned to an input, allowing concept-level relationships to contribute to the detection decision. Because those constraints involve understandable concepts, the approach also offers a more explainable basis for identifying unusual inputs.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report significant improvements for a wide range of existing detectors while retaining computational efficiency. They also introduce and evaluate a simple algorithm that learns logical constraints from data. Together, these contributions make probabilistic logic both an additional detection signal and a source of interpretability, with the reported gains supporting its use alongside established statistical detectors.
icml-2025-improving-out-of-distribution-.tldr: Markov logic networks improve existing out-of-distribution detectors by adding efficient probabilistic reasoning over understandable concepts.

paragraphs: Lexico compresses the key-value cache used by language models through sparse coding. Its central finding is that cache contents can be accurately approximated using combinations of only a few elements from a small dictionary. The dictionary contains 4k atoms and is input-agnostic, supporting compression across different prompts, tasks, and models.

The method uses orthogonal matching pursuit to construct these sparse approximations. Controlling how many dictionary elements participate gives direct control over sparsity and therefore flexible compression ratios. This makes the size of the representation an explicit adjustable quantity within the compression method.

On GSM8K, evaluations across Mistral, Llama 3, and Qwen2.5 retain 90–95% of original performance while using 15–25% of the full cache memory. The paper reports better results than quantization and token eviction methods. Lexico also remains effective in low-memory settings where 2-bit quantization fails, with up to 1.7 times better compression on LongBench and GSM8K while retaining high accuracy. These findings support sparse dictionary representations as a useful option for severe cache-memory constraints.
icml-2025-lexico-extreme-kv-cache-compre.tldr: Lexico compresses language-model KV caches with sparse dictionary representations, retaining much of the original performance at substantially lower memory use.

paragraphs: Linear bandit methods use features to guide repeated decisions, but some reward-relevant features may be hidden. Ignoring their influence can lead to regret that grows linearly with the number of decisions. This paper develops a framework and algorithm that account for partial feature observability and provide a sublinear regret guarantee.

The algorithm augments the observed features with basis vectors orthogonal to their row space and introduces a doubly robust estimator. The augmentation supplies additional representational directions beyond those covered by the observed features. The resulting method does not require prior knowledge of the unobserved feature space, including when that space expands as more features become hidden.

Its regret bound grows roughly as the square root of (d + d_h) times T, up to logarithmic factors. Here d counts observed-feature dimensions, while d_h captures how the hidden feature space relates to the observed one. The guarantee therefore reflects the problem's intrinsic hidden-feature difficulty. Numerical experiments report better performance than non-contextual bandits and linear bandit algorithms that rely only on observed features.
icml-2025-linear-bandits-with-partially-.tldr: Feature augmentation and a doubly robust estimator enable sublinear regret in linear bandits with partially hidden features.

paragraphs: When a model learns tasks sequentially, its internal representations can change in ways that undermine earlier learning. This paper studies that hidden-layer form of forgetting. It introduces representation discrepancy, a metric comparing the representation spaces produced by two snapshots of a model during continual learning.

The metric is designed to serve as an effective surrogate for representation forgetting while remaining manageable for mathematical analysis. This matters because a measure that can be analyzed provides a route from observing representational change to understanding its dynamics. The paper uses this route to develop a theoretical account of how forgetting varies with network structure.

The analysis finds that forgetting becomes faster and more pronounced at higher layer indices, while increasing network width slows the process. Experiments on real image datasets, including Split-CIFAR100 and ImageNet1K, support these theoretical findings. The contribution therefore combines a measurement tool with structural insights: depth within the network and network width help explain differences in representational forgetting in the analyzed and evaluated settings.
icml-2025-measuring-representational-shi.tldr: Representation discrepancy makes hidden-layer forgetting analytically tractable and reveals how layer position and network width affect its dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper models chain-of-thought reasoning as a Markov process with regions that are easy to move within but difficult to leave. Routine reasoning steps create densely connected clusters. Harder moves, such as selecting a relevant theorem, form sparse connections between clusters. This metastable structure explains how progress can depend on rare transitions.

Within this framework, the authors prove that a search protocol rewarding sparse connections reduces the expected number of steps needed to reach other clusters. They also establish a limit on reasoning when a model uses only local information from the pretrained graph. The benefit of search is therefore tied to finding consequential connections that local information alone cannot adequately exploit.

The paper further shows how information acquired through search can improve a reasoning model. Policy-gradient fine-tuning can encourage the pretrained model to take sparse connections, while distillation can transfer a compressed representation of the metastable dynamics into a smaller model. These are theoretical results within the proposed framework, linking inference-time search to subsequent reinforcement learning and more efficient representations of reasoning.
icml-2025-metastable-dynamics-of-chain-o.tldr: A metastable model of reasoning explains provable benefits of searching for rare transitions and transferring that knowledge through fine-tuning or distillation.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy can affect several stakeholders differently, making the choice of an overall objective consequential. This paper studies generalized p-means, a family of social welfare functions that includes egalitarian, Nash, and utilitarian welfare. Changing p can substantially alter both the structure of an optimal policy and the outcomes it produces.

The proposed response is to compute a portfolio of policies covering these different choices. An alpha-approximate portfolio provides approximately optimal options across the family for every p from negative infinity to one. This turns a potentially difficult choice of welfare function into a policy space that decision-makers can inspect through a representative set of alternatives.

The authors propose portfolio-construction algorithms and prove trade-offs involving approximation quality, the number of policies retained, and computational efficiency. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the portfolios effectively summarize policies induced by different p values. The approach supports exploration of stakeholder trade-offs while leaving the choice of welfare preferences with the decision-maker.
icml-2025-navigating-the-social-welfare-.tldr: Approximately optimal policy portfolios help decision-makers explore how different social welfare preferences change reinforcement-learning outcomes.

paragraphs: Skills let an agent make decisions over extended stretches of activity, which can help with long-horizon tasks. Choosing a fixed duration for every skill, however, can carry the agent past useful opportunities to reconsider its behavior. This paper focuses on learning when a skill should end so that important decision points remain available.

Novelty-based Decision Point Identification, or NBDI, learns a termination condition using a module that evaluates novelty in state-action pairs. The module draws on the agent's experience data to identify decision points. In the setting of skill extraction from task-agnostic demonstrations, this makes the timing of decisions something learned from experience rather than determined solely by a fixed skill length.

The authors report that NBDI outperforms previous baselines on complex, long-horizon tasks. It also remains effective when downstream tasks have substantially different environment configurations. These results support the importance of skill boundaries: identifying where an agent should regain decision-making control can improve the usefulness of learned skills and their application in varied environments.
icml-2025-nbdi-a-simple-and-effective-te.tldr: NBDI learns novelty-based skill termination conditions to preserve useful decision points in long-horizon tasks.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter extends averaging to probability distributions using optimal transport. Computing an unregularized barycenter becomes challenging beyond one dimension, so practical methods often introduce entropic regularization. This paper introduces WDHA to compute the exact, unregularized barycenter for probability densities discretized on an m-point grid.

WDHA is a primal-dual algorithm that alternates between two optimization geometries. It uses Wasserstein geometry for the barycenter subproblem and Sobolev geometry for the dual Kantorovich potential subproblem. The paper reports nearly linear time complexity, O(m log m), and linear space complexity, O(m), making the grid size central to its computational scaling.

Under stated reasonable assumptions and an appropriate step size, the authors establish convergence rates and iteration complexity to a stationary point. That guarantee should be distinguished from an unconditional guarantee of reaching a global optimum. Evaluations on synthetic and real two-dimensional data, including 1024-by-1024 images, demonstrate better computational efficacy, scalability, and accuracy than existing Sinkhorn-type algorithms. The results support the value of matching the two subproblems to different optimization geometries.
icml-2025-optimal-transport-barycenter-v.tldr: WDHA tackles unregularized Wasserstein barycenters with complementary optimization geometries and conditional convergence guarantees to a stationary point.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from offline data must estimate action values using a limited record of experience. Predictions outside that data range can be inaccurate, producing Q-value extrapolation errors. This paper first shows that linear extrapolation of the Q-function beyond the available data is particularly problematic, motivating a different shape for those out-of-range predictions.

The proposed approach guides Q-values to decrease gradually outside the data range. It combines reward scaling with layer normalization, called RS-LN, and a mechanism that penalizes infeasible actions, called PA. Together these components form PARS. Their shared purpose is to influence value estimates where extrapolation would otherwise make unsupported actions appear attractive.

The authors evaluate PARS during both offline training and subsequent online fine-tuning. On the D4RL benchmark, they report better performance than state-of-the-art algorithms across the evaluated tasks, including notable success on AntMaze Ultra. The findings connect a specific diagnosis of extrapolation behavior with practical value-estimation changes, showing benefits in learning from fixed data and in continuing to learn through interaction.
icml-2025-penalizing-infeasible-actions-.tldr: PARS combines reward scaling, layer normalization, and infeasible-action penalties to reduce harmful Q-value extrapolation in offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Where a Transformer places layer normalization affects how signals and gradients behave during training. This paper analyzes that placement question, including the familiar Pre-LN and Post-LN strategies and a third design called Peri-LN. The latter places normalization around the periphery of sublayers and had already appeared in some open-source models without much explanation.

The authors develop an analytical account of how these strategies shape activation variance and gradient propagation. These quantities connect architectural choices to training behavior: activation variance describes the spread of internal signals, while gradient propagation concerns how learning signals travel through the network. The analysis aims to explain the mechanisms behind Peri-LN's promising behavior.

Experiments on Transformers with up to 3.2 billion parameters support the theoretical account. Peri-LN consistently produces more balanced variance growth, steadier gradient flow, and stable convergence in those evaluations. The results support broader consideration of this normalization placement for large-scale Transformers. They also provide a more explicit basis for understanding a design choice that had been adopted with limited explanation.
icml-2025-peri-ln-revisiting-normalizati.tldr: Peri-LN's placement of normalization around Transformer sublayers supports balanced activation variance and steadier training in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent updates selected coordinates of an optimization problem. Two common selection rules choose coordinates uniformly at random or follow random permutations of the indices. Although experiments have often favored random permutations, establishing a clear theoretical advantage has been difficult, even for structured positive-definite quadratic objectives.

This paper proves a strict separation for a class of quadratics with permutation-invariant structure. For every individual problem in that class, the upper bound on the random-permutation method's contraction rate is below the lower bound for uniform random sampling. Because smaller contraction rates correspond to faster convergence, the bounds establish a performance advantage throughout this particular class.

The authors also conjecture that this structured class contains the worst-case examples for random-permutation coordinate descent among all positive-definite quadratics. If that conjecture holds, combining it with their lower bound for uniform sampling extends the result to the broader class. The paper therefore contributes both a proven instance-by-instance comparison in a restricted setting and a conditional route toward a more general explanation.
icml-2025-provable-benefit-of-random-per.tldr: Random-permutation coordinate descent has a provably better contraction rate for a structured quadratic class, with broader implications contingent on a conjecture.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce repetitive outputs or recreate images from their training data. SPELL addresses both issues by steering generation away from a reference collection of images. It operates on pretrained diffusion models, modifying the sampling trajectory rather than requiring a new model to be trained.

The method adds repulsion terms to the diffusion stochastic differential equation when a trajectory is expected to finish too close to a protected image. These terms are inactive most of the time and become even sparser toward the end of generation. The reference collection can remain fixed, or it can change to include expected outputs from the current batch and images from earlier batches.

The authors report improved diversity with only marginal changes in FID, alongside better comparative performance than other recent training-free diversity methods. They also demonstrate shielding against a reference collection containing all 1.2 million ImageNet images. The results show how selective intervention during sampling can support both output diversity and avoidance of a large protected collection.
icml-2025-shielded-diffusion-generating-.tldr: SPELL selectively repels diffusion sampling trajectories from reference images to improve diversity and support protected-image avoidance.

paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks aim to sample graphs in proportion to their rewards. Graph symmetries can interfere with that goal by causing inaccuracies in state-transition probability calculations. This paper identifies the resulting systematic sampling biases in both atom-based and fragment-based graph generation, making symmetry relevant to more than one construction scheme.

Symmetry-Aware GFlowNets, or SA-GFN, incorporate corrections through reward scaling. Instead of relying on explicit state-transition computations to handle the bias, the method builds the correction into the rewards used for learning. The key change is therefore in the learning objective's reward structure, where symmetry information adjusts the signal guiding graph generation.

The empirical results show unbiased sampling, improved diversity, and consistent generation of high-reward graphs closely matching the desired distribution. These findings concern more than the quality of individual generated graphs: they address whether the overall collection appears with the intended frequencies. The paper presents reward-based symmetry correction as a way to improve that distributional match while avoiding explicit transition calculations.
icml-2025-symmetry-aware-gflownets-12809.tldr: SA-GFN corrects symmetry-related graph-sampling biases through reward scaling, improving empirical diversity and agreement with the target distribution.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to produce policies that work on previously unseen tasks. Context-based methods represent tasks using latent variables, but those representations can struggle when new tasks fall outside the training distribution. Task-Aware Virtual Training, or TAVT, addresses this generalization problem by focusing on how task characteristics are represented and preserved.

TAVT uses metric-based representation learning to capture characteristics of both training tasks and out-of-distribution tasks. It preserves those characteristics in virtual tasks used by the method. This makes task representation central to virtual training: the virtual tasks retain the properties the algorithm is trying to learn about, rather than treating their representation as an incidental detail.

The method also introduces state regularization to mitigate overestimation errors in environments where states vary. Numerical evaluations across MuJoCo and MetaWorld environments report significant improvements in generalization to out-of-distribution tasks. Together, the results support combining task-aware representations, virtual training, and control of overestimation to improve performance beyond the tasks represented in training.
icml-2025-task-aware-virtual-training-en.tldr: TAVT combines task-aware virtual training and state regularization to improve meta-reinforcement learning on out-of-distribution tasks.

paragraphs: A vision-language navigation agent deployed in an unfamiliar environment may need to adapt as it operates. This paper argues that useful adaptation should accommodate different outcomes, learn through environmental interaction, and balance learning new behavior with maintaining stability. FeedTTA implements this view through feedback-based reinforcement learning during deployment.

The agent receives a single binary signal after each navigation episode indicating success or failure. FeedTTA learns to maximize this episodic feedback, making the signal directly relevant to whether navigation succeeded. The framework also includes gradient regularization that uses the binary structure of the feedback to balance plasticity and stability during adaptation.

Experiments on challenging navigation benchmarks show strong adaptability. On REVERIE, FeedTTA even outperforms state-of-the-art offline training methods using a single stream of learning. The reported finding supports the value of adapting through simple outcome feedback rather than relying entirely on behavior learned before deployment. Its adaptation setup specifically assumes that success-or-failure feedback is available after each episode.
icml-2025-test-time-adaptation-for-onlin.tldr: FeedTTA adapts navigation agents during deployment using binary episode feedback and gradient regularization to balance learning with stability.

paragraphs: Surface-mesh neural networks can make physical analysis more efficient, but a surface description can overlook an object's thickness. Opposing surfaces may behave similarly even though the mesh contains no internal edges connecting them. This paper addresses that gap with T-EMNN, a network designed to capture thickness effects while retaining the efficiency of surface meshes.

The framework integrates thickness information and introduces data-driven coordinates for encoding spatial information. These coordinates preserve E(3)-equivariance or invariance, giving the representation specified consistency properties under spatial transformations. Thickness awareness and geometric consistency are therefore built into the same framework for analyzing three-dimensional objects.

On a real-world industrial dataset, T-EMNN demonstrates superior performance in predicting three-dimensional deformation at individual mesh nodes. The reported results show that it captures thickness effects while maintaining computational efficiency. The significance is that relationships between opposing surfaces contribute useful information for deformation prediction, even when the underlying representation retains the computational advantages of a surface mesh.
icml-2025-thickness-aware-e-3-equivarian.tldr: T-EMNN incorporates object thickness into geometrically consistent surface-mesh networks to improve deformation prediction while retaining computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models generate discrete data by filling missing tokens and can choose the order in which to do so. That flexibility creates a training challenge: the model must learn an exponentially large collection of possible infilling problems. This paper examines the tension between difficult training subproblems and freedom over the generation order.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that masked diffusion training encounters computationally intractable subproblems compared with autoregressive training. At inference time, however, a suitable adaptive ordering strategy can avoid hard subproblems. The next token to decode becomes a consequential choice that can make better use of a pretrained model's capabilities.

On logic puzzles such as Sudoku, adaptive inference raises solving accuracy in pretrained masked diffusion models from below 7% to approximately 90%. It also exceeds autoregressive models explicitly trained through teacher forcing to learn the correct decoding order. These results demonstrate a substantial benefit from adaptive token ordering in the evaluated setting and explain how inference flexibility can counter some of the difficulties encountered during training.
icml-2025-train-for-the-worst-plan-for-t.tldr: Adaptive token ordering lets masked diffusion models avoid difficult infilling subproblems and dramatically improves reported logic-puzzle accuracy.

paragraphs: Time-series domain adaptation must account for changes in both temporal patterns and individual channels. Conventional pseudo-labeling can miss these structures and assign poor labels to target-domain data. TransPL instead models the source domain's joint distribution of observations and classes through transitions between discrete codes derived from time-series patches.

Vector quantization supplies the codes, and TransPL constructs transition matrices separately for classes and channels. These matrices describe temporal code changes in the source data. The method then applies Bayes' rule and channel-weighted class-conditional likelihoods to generate target pseudo-labels, making both temporal transitions and channel contributions explicit in the labeling process.

Across four time-series adaptation benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art pseudo-labeling methods, including 6.1% accuracy improvement and 4.9% F1 improvement. The approach also supports different adaptation scenarios, including weak supervision. Its learned transition matrices provide interpretable information about the adaptation process, connecting pseudo-label decisions to identifiable temporal patterns rather than leaving their basis entirely implicit.
icml-2025-transpl-vq-code-transition-mat.tldr: TransPL uses class- and channel-specific code transitions to generate more accurate, interpretable pseudo-labels for time-series domain adaptation.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo samplers depend strongly on how their Markov kernels are tuned. For unadjusted kernels, familiar objectives such as acceptance rate or expected squared jump distance are no longer applicable. End-to-end gradient optimization offers another route, but it can be expensive even when the only parameters being tuned are step sizes.

This paper proposes adapting kernels by minimizing incremental Kullback–Leibler divergence between proposal and target paths. The objective measures mismatch at the path level and supports a general tuning framework. For step sizes, the authors provide an algorithm that requires neither gradients nor additional tuning and applies to kernels such as Langevin Monte Carlo.

They also develop a specialized scheme for kinetic Langevin Monte Carlo within SMC. Their implementations produce an entire schedule of tuned parameters for a cost comparable to only a few ordinary SMC runs, substantially below that of gradient-based approaches. The contribution is a practical adaptation objective paired with inexpensive procedures, making kernel tuning less costly in the settings considered.
icml-2025-tuning-sequential-monte-carlo-.tldr: Incremental path-divergence minimization enables inexpensive tuning of SMC kernels without gradient-based optimization for step sizes.
